analysis.one_liner: Bars federal judges from owning stocks, applies ethics rules to the Supreme Court, and opens secret court settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of its six committees, dying at the end of the 118th Congress with 44 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks, bonds, hedge funds, and private businesses, while allowing them a government-run diversified fund instead. It would apply the judges' Code of Conduct to the Supreme Court for the first time by law, create a formal process for complaints against justices, require judges to publicly list their recusal conflicts, and ban gifts connected to privately funded judicial seminars. It would also limit courts' ability to seal evidence of public health and safety hazards in settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Litigants and the general public. People who sue corporations would no longer face judges who own stock in the company they are suing, and evidence of public health and safety hazards could no longer be hidden by secret settlement agreements. The public would gain searchable online lists of each judge's conflicts, posted speeches, live audio of appellate arguments, and a formal complaint process for Supreme Court misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Litigants, court employees, and the public

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits judges and justices from owning or trading stocks, bonds, hedge funds, derivatives, and other securities, and from owning commercial real estate, closely held businesses, or serving on for-profit boards, with civil fines up to $50,000 per violation [S3].

Requires each judge and justice to file a public, searchable list of every association or financial interest — including a spouse's or child's — that would require recusal, and requires justices to give written public explanations for recusal decisions [S3].

Bars judges from soliciting or accepting gifts connected to private judicial seminars — the all-expenses-paid industry-sponsored events that have drawn criticism — and creates a publicly funded Judicial Education Fund for approved seminars instead [S3].

Restricts courts from entering or enforcing protective orders and settlement agreements that conceal information relevant to public health or safety, and from barring parties from reporting hazards to federal or state regulators [S3].

Extends the Code of Conduct for United States Judges to Supreme Court justices, creates a complaint process for justices including a Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee under House Judiciary, and requires annual reports on judicial misconduct complaints to be made public [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Judges and justices who would have to divest stock holdings, hedge funds, and business interests into a government-run diversified account; corporations that fund luxury judicial seminars and those that rely on sealed settlements to bury evidence of unsafe products; and, in the bill's critics' view, judicial independence, if Congress enforces an ethics code on the third branch.
analysis.who_pays_short: Judges with stock portfolios and seminar-sponsoring industries

drawbacks.text: Mandatory divestment of all securities could make the bench less attractive to experienced candidates from the private sector, and the bill's $50,000 civil fines for stock ownership are strict — though the bill softens this by creating a government-run diversified investment account judges may use instead [S3].

Applying a congressionally mandated code of conduct and a House-run review committee to the Supreme Court raises separation-of-powers questions; critics argue Congress cannot discipline the third branch this way, and the bill itself acknowledges the constitutional question by relying partly on a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that justices adhere to the Code under their 'good behaviour' tenure [S3].

The new Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee would operate largely in secret, with a general prohibition on public disclosure of complaint information unless the committee votes to disclose it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core conflict-of-interest and transparency provisions are straightforward: a judge who owns stock in a company has a reason to rule for it, and the bill removes that reason while leaving judges a clean way to invest. The strongest good-faith objections are the practical ones — strict divestment could deter candidates, and Congress disciplining the Supreme Court raises constitutional questions the bill only partly answers. The public-health sealing restrictions are the most significant for ordinary people, since secret settlements have historically kept unsafe products on the market. On balance the benefits to court users and the public outweigh the costs, though the enforcement machinery is heavy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on June 9, 2023, with 43 Democratic cosponsors, during a period of intense public scrutiny of Supreme Court ethics following reporting on undisclosed gifts and travel to justices [S1][S3].

The bill was referred to six committees — Judiciary, Oversight and Accountability, Rules, Financial Services, Agriculture, and House Administration — for consideration of the provisions in each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
No committee held a markup, hearing, or vote, and the House never considered the bill; it received no action after its introduction and referrals [S5].
All 44 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal judges and justices keep their existing disclosure and investment practices, industries that fund judicial seminars and rely on sealed settlements keep the status quo, and no one else — the bill's reforms died without ever being debated.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Judicial Ethics and Anti-Corruption Act of 2023 in the House on June 9, 2023.

for.name: 43 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, including Reps. Nadler, Khanna, Porter, Tlaib, Schakowsky, Schiff, and others [S3][S4].

against.name: House committee chairs (Judiciary, Oversight, Rules, Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration)
against.role: Chairs of the six committees of referral
against.what_they_did: None of the six committees referred the bill took it up; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled, so the bill died without floor action [S5].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the majority did not bring it to the floor [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 44 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill never reached a recorded vote [S4].

industries.industry: Industries that fund private judicial seminars
industries.note: The bill bans judges from accepting gifts in connection with private judicial seminars and replaces industry-paid junkets with a taxpayer-funded Judicial Education Fund. Corporate-sponsored seminars have been a channel through which litigants and their allies fund luxury travel for judges who may later hear their cases.

industries.industry: Companies relying on sealed settlements (product liability, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, autos)
industries.note: The bill restricts courts from sealing evidence or settlement terms relevant to public health or safety, so companies could no longer buy secrecy over hazards alongside a settlement. This means more unsafe-product information reaching regulators and consumers.

industries.industry: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices (as officeholders with investment income)
industries.note: Judges would have to divest individual stocks, hedge funds, trusts with securities, and business ownership into a government-run diversified account, and publicly list recusal conflicts. The bill keeps judges a way to invest, so the loss is flexibility and privacy, not the ability to save for retirement.

With public recusal lists and a ban on judge stock ownership, companies would no longer draw judges who own shares in them, and could no longer enforce agreements blocking disclosure of hazards to regulators.
